‘Very difficult to bridge that divide’: Watt
Cabinet minister
Murray Watt
says it’s increasingly difficult to bridge the divide between nations on climate policy after a pretty frustrating and disappointing COP summit that didn’t reach a final agreement.
It’s obviously a very deeply disappointing outcome that the cover decision was not agreed to by all nations.
I think what this shows is a very challenging international environment at the moment to reach agreement on almost anything and particularly a situation like this where you’ve got fossil fuel producers on the one hand and other countries that are experiencing very serious impacts from climate change. That’s a very wide divide to be bridged and it’s very disappointing that that wasn’t possible.
We’re seeing much greater defence engagement between Australia and Japan, Australia and the Philippines, and the Philippines and Japan.
Even though I think it doesn’t quite come across in its overall score, that US defence relationship in the region is stronger, which is helping Australia.

items.title: Netanyahu, Eisenkot parties end talks without deal on forming government
items.content:
Netanyahu, Eisenkot parties end talks without deal on forming government
The parties of caretaker Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot concluded a new round of talks on Sunday without reaching an agreement on a possible coalition government, which would require concessions from both sides.
Delegations from Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Netanyahu’s Likud met for four hours at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, following a first round of discussions last Sunday.
“The latest round of coalition talks… has concluded. The two sides outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues and discussed them in detail,” the two parties said in a joint statement.
“A follow-up meeting will be held,” they added, without specifying a date or revealing any other details.
A former army chief of staff, Eisenkot has until 6 December to form a government, with the possibility of a 14‑day extension, after October elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority.
His 48-member bloc, which needs 61 lawmakers to reach a majority, remains divided over whether to build a coalition through an alliance with ultra‑Orthodox parties, a rapprochement with Arab parties, or a national unity government with Likud.
Netanyahu is pushing for a national unity government, which could see a rotation of the premiership between the two men.
Pedestrians walk past an advertisement featuring Benjamin Netanyahu (R) of the Likud party and leader of the Yashar party Gadi Eisenkot, along a street in Ramat Gan on 23 September 2026 (AFP)

items.title: Two Palestinians killed by Israeli fire in northern and central Gaza
items.content:
Two Palestinians killed by Israeli fire in northern and central Gaza
Israeli forces killed two Palestinians in separate attacks in the Gaza Strip on Sunday, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
One was shot dead by Israeli gunfire in Jabalia, north of Gaza, on Sunday evening.
Earlier in the evening, an Israeli quadcopter drone struck and killed another Palestinian in eastern Deir al-Balah, in central Gaza.
Israel has killed more than 1,600 Palestinians in Gaza since the ceasefire agreement of October 2025.
At least 74,742 Palestinians have been killed and 176,227 wounded since the war began in October 2023.

items.content:
No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia
A suspected Ukrainian drone attack caused an explosion on a Russian warship docked at the naval base in the Libyan port city of Benghazi, Libyan officials have said.
The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy warship, and ignited a fire at the naval base, they said. Several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, the officials told the Associated Press.

items.title: Bahrain says Iranian strike wounds two, one critically
items.content:
Bahrain says Iranian strike wounds two, one critically
Bahrain said on Sunday that two people were wounded in an Iranian strike the previous day on “a civilian industrial site” in the Gulf kingdom, which has faced several attacks this week.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has repeatedly said they targeted US facilities in Bahrain, where Iranian strikes resumed earlier in November.
"In the wake of the criminal Iranian attacks suffered yesterday (Saturday) by the Kingdom of Bahrain… a Bahraini national with a disability was wounded," Bahrain's interior ministry said on X.
"His condition is stable. A Pakistani resident was also wounded and is in critical condition."
Residents had seen smoke rising above Sitra Island, east of Manama, which hosts several industrial facilities, including a refinery operated by the state-owned oil company Bapco, AFP reported.
In a statement carried by Iranian state media on Saturday evening, the IRGC said they had attacked US Patriot air defence systems with missiles and drones at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain, in response to the “continued violations of the airspace” of the Islamic Republic.
Bahrain's foreign ministry dismissed the IRGC's account, saying the site hit was purely civilian and industrial, calling the attack a direct danger to civilians and a violation of the kingdom's sovereignty.
Bahrain's neighbour Saudi Arabia on Sunday also condemned Tehran for its attacks on Gulf countries.
The Saudi foreign ministry expressed on X "the strongest condemnation and denunciation... of the criminal Iranian attacks against a civilian industrial facility in the brotherly Kingdom of Bahrain".
As a result of the heinous Iranian attacks on Bahrain yesterday, a Bahraini citizen with disabilities sustained injuries and is in stable condition, while a Pakistani resident was also injured and is in critical condition. Both are receiving treatment in the hospital. #Bahrain #MOI
— وزارة الداخلية - Ministry of Interior (@moi_bahrain)
November 22, 2026

items.title: Iran unveils new launcher that can fire two missiles at once
items.content:
Iran unveils new launcher that can fire two missiles at once
Iran has unveiled a new missile launcher, as senior military commanders touted the Islamic Republic's capabilities in defiant messages to the United States.
"A launcher capable of firing two liquid-propellant missiles simultaneously was unveiled for the first time," Iranian state television reported on Saturday.
State television broadcast footage of Ahmad Vahidi, commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and Majid Mousavi, head of the IRGC's Aerospace Force, touring an underground missile base.
The two commanders were shown riding on top of a vehicle through long tunnels lined with missiles, launchers and other military equipment.
"The damage suffered by our enemy is only the beginning. We shall witness their humiliation," Vahidi said.
"Our capabilities have grown during the last two conflicts, and our high-performance weaponry can intimidate the enemy," said Mousavi.
During the US-Israeli war on Iran, strikes targeted the country's missile capabilities and hit its nuclear sites for a second time, though the extent of the damage remains unclear.
Earlier this month, the IRGC unveiled what it described as new underground "missile cities" housing ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as launchers.
Ahmad Vahidi, commander of the IRGC, and Majid Mousavi, head of the IRGC's Aerospace Force, visit one of the Guards' underground "missile cities" on 10 November 2026 (Tasnim)

items.title: Libya's eastern government suspects drone attack caused explosion on Russian ship
items.content:
By Ayman Al-Warfali
Nov 22 (Reuters) - A suspected drone attack caused an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya, the country's eastern-based government said on Sunday after a preliminary investigation.
No one has claimed responsibility for the suspected attack, and there was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Ukrainian forces have repeatedly used naval drones and missiles to target Russian warships and naval facilities in the Black Sea.

items.title: Drone strikes hit homes, UN building in Sudan's capital
items.content:
Drones struck Sudan's capital Khartoum, damaging residential homes and a United Nations building on Sunday, witnesses and the world organisation said.
Explosions were heard in the area around Khartoum airport and other parts of the city from around 2:00 am until approximately 4:30 am.
A drone strike completely destroyed a house, a witness said, while a Sudanese army source said the drones had been launched from Ethiopia.

items.title: Two supertankers hit mines near Hormuz, Iranian navy says
items.content:
Two supertankers hit mines near Hormuz, Iranian navy says
Iran's navy said on Sunday that two supertankers hit naval mines and caught fire after entering a "restricted area" east of the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian media reported.
According to the Fars news agency, the navy said the tankers had switched off their detection and navigation systems and struck the mines north of Ghanam Island.
Both vessels reportedly stopped moving.
Supertankers usually carry two million barrels of oil or more, about twice as much as a standard tanker.
The navy also warned that relying on "smugglers such as CENTCOM", referring to US Central Command, would result in "nothing but heavy losses".
UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) also said on Sunday it had received a report of an incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman.
It gave no further details, saying only that authorities were aware and an investigation was under way. It was unclear whether the incident involved either of the tankers Iran described.
British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh swam in the waters of the Strait of Hormuz to highlight the "devastating environmental consequences of war" on 21 November 2026 (Lewis Pugh Foundation / AFP)

items.title: From arson to land seizures: Settlers tighten grip on Palestinian villages near Ramallah
items.content:
From arson to land seizures: Settlers tighten grip on Palestinian villages near Ramallah
Submitted by
Fayha Shalash
on
Sun, 11/22/2026 - 13:25
The attacks come amid a sharp rise in settler violence during the olive harvest, with the UN documenting a record 467 incidents in October
An Israeli settler stands between Israeli forces and Palestinians protesting an alleged arson attack in Idna, west of Hebron, occupied West Bank, 5 June 2026 (Hazem Bader/AFP)
Off
In a series of coordinated attacks across several villages near the city of Ramallah in the central occupied West Bank,
Israeli
settlers torched
Palestinian
vehicles between Saturday evening and Sunday morning.
The settlers also spray-painted racist slogans on the walls of homes in the three villages, calling for the killing of Arabs and for revenge against them.
Rafat Abu Musa, head of the village council of Deir al-Sudan, north of Ramallah, told Middle East Eye that settlers infiltrated the southern part of the village at 11.30pm on Saturday and burned down two vehicles.
The settlers spray-painted slogans in Hebrew on the walls of nearby houses, he said, adding that the same area had been targeted by a similar attack two months ago, during which a vehicle was set on fire.
The settlers, he said, came from a newly built outpost on the summit of Jabal al-Ras, located in the neighbouring village of Umm Safa.
"The fire department was delayed in reaching the scene because they require coordination with the Israeli army; by the time they arrived, the vehicles had already been reduced to ashes," he said.
According to Abu Musa, some five months ago, the settlers seized "an entire mountain" in the southern part of the village, where they established an outpost and constructed roads.
The outpost has deprived residents of access to more than half of the village’s olive trees, as settlers assault the residents and prevent them from approaching their own land, he said.
"This fierce onslaught is being directed by extremist Israeli ministers; these are systematic and recurring attacks," Abu Musa said.
The area where the vehicles were torched is classified as 'Area A'. Under the Oslo Accords, the region is supposed to be under exclusive Palestinian control.
Fake investigations
A few hours after the attack in Abu Musa's village, settlers set fire to seven vehicles in the town of Kafr Malik, east of Ramallah.
More than ten settlers infiltrated the northern part of the town, arriving from an outpost they had established between Kafr Malik and al-Mughayyir; a journey that required them to trek for at least an hour along a rugged mountain path, Jihad Qaq, a resident, told Middle East Eye.
'Jewish terrorism in every sense': Eisenkot blames Smotrich and Ben Gvir for settler attacks
Read More »
He said that the settlers reached Palestinian homes, set the vehicles on fire and wrote racist slogans on the walls of the houses before withdrawing.
"An hour after the attack, the Israeli army stormed the town, forced the civil defence crews who were in the process of extinguishing the fires to leave and drove away the residents."
"They conducted an investigation, but then withdrew without any results," Qaq said.
He said that the village is constantly subjected to harassment by settlers, who, a year and a half ago, burned vehicles in the southern part of the area and killed three young men.
"Settler herders have prevented more than 70 percent of the Palestinian olive harvesters from reaching their land this year, assaulting and beating them," he said.
According to data from the Commission Against the Wall and Settlements, attacks by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank saw a marked increase this past October, coinciding with the olive harvest season.
Settlers carried out 1,369 attacks during the month, a 112 percent rise compared to September, which saw 647 such incidents.
Relentless attacks
Meanwhile, in the eastern part of the village of Deir Abu Mashal west of Ramallah, classified as 'Area B', settlers burned eight vehicles and wrote racist slogans.
Jamil Musa, head of the village council, said that the settlers arrived from an outpost they had established a few months ago, one of several such outposts they have set up in the vicinity of the village.
Israeli settlers kill Palestinian grandmother in her home in Jericho
Read More »
He said that the attack took place at 2.30am, and the group, consisting of eight to 10 individuals, withdrew from the village after painting racist slogans.
"The Israeli army raided the village and promised to launch an investigation, but nothing has come of it. They also told us that the Israeli police would follow up, but they have yet to arrive," he stated.
Two months ago, settlers set fire to vehicles in the village. In June 2025, they assaulted several families and beat five young men, leaving them with serious injuries.
Residents are unable to access nearly half of the village’s land for the olive harvest due to attacks by settlers, who have been assaulting Palestinians farmers.
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) documented 467 settler attacks that resulted in injuries or property damage during the month of October alone, the highest monthly figure since the organisation began tracking such incidents in 2006.
Over the course of the year, from the beginning of January through 19 October, Ocha recorded 2,159 settler attacks, an average of 7.4 incidents per day, compared to a daily average of five attacks throughout 2025.
According to Ocha, these attacks were particularly concentrated during the olive harvest season.
Between 1 September and 19 October, 272 attacks linked to the harvest were recorded, resulting in the killing of one Palestinian, injuries to 200 others and the destruction of more than 3,200 olive trees.

items.title: Houthis say they attacked Saudi Arabia's Rabigh oil refinery
items.content:
Houthis say they attacked Saudi Arabia's Rabigh oil refinery
Yemen's Houthis said on Sunday they had attacked
Saudi Arabia
's Rabigh oil refinery on the kingdom's Red Sea coast north of Jeddah.
Saudi authorities did not immediately comment.
The Houthis have claimed a string of attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure in recent months.
The kingdom's Red Sea coast has become increasingly important to its oil exports, with Riyadh using its East-West pipeline to move crude from the Gulf to western ports, rather than through the Strait of Hormuz.

items.title: Theresa May’s blast from the past calls Tories back to their unhappy place | Peter Walker
items.content:
Conservatives may instinctively want to push back against closer EU ties, but they have to train their focus elsewhere
Anyone who accidentally switched to BBC One at about 9.45am on Sunday to be greeted by Theresa May
awkwardly espousing
the virtues of Brexit could have been forgiven for thinking they had woken up in around 2018 – and not being especially pleased at the idea.
This is one of the problems now facing May’s party. For all that it is a reflex action for Conservatives to push back against closer ties with the EU, Andy Burnham’s decision to pursue such a course plunges them back into their own unhappy place.

items.title: مستوطنون إسرائيليون يحرقون ممتلكات فلسطينية في أربع قرى بالضفة الغربية
items.content:
مستوطنون إسرائيليون يحرقون ممتلكات فلسطينية في أربع قرى بالضفة الغربية
أضرم مستوطنون إسرائيليون، ليلة السبت إلى الأحد، النار في مركبات وممتلكات فلسطينية في أربع قرى بالضفة الغربية المحتلة، وكتبوا شعارات وعبارات تهديد باللغة العبرية على جدران المنازل، وفق مصادر فلسطينية و أخرى من السلطات الإسرائيلية. وتعتبر هذه الحادثة هي الأحدث في سلسلة من الاعتداءات التي تشهدها المنطقة وسط تصاعد عنف المستوطنين.

👈 اقرأ المزيد: https://f24.my/CIft.g

items.title: فرنسا: محافظ يطلب إعفائه من مهامه بعد تحقيق قضائي حول تسريب معلومات سرية لحزب مارين لوبان
items.content:
فرنسا: محافظ يطلب إعفائه من مهامه بعد تحقيق قضائي حول تسريب معلومات سرية لحزب مارين لوبان
طلب الأمين العام السابق لوزارة الداخلية الفرنسية، هوغ موتو، إعفائه من مهامه كمحافظ لإقليم سنتر-فال-دو-لوار (وسط فرنسا) بعد أن وجد نفسه في قلب تحقيق قضائي على خلفية شبهات بشأن دوره في تسريب معلومات سرية إلى حزب "التجمع الوطني" اليميني المتطرف. وترتبط هذه المعلومات بتحقيقات قضائية تتعلق بحزب مارين لوبان، التي تضعها استطلاعات الرأي ضمن أبرز المرشحين للانتخابات الرئاسية الفرنسية المقررة عام 2027.

👈 اقرأ المزيد: https://f24.my/CIfp.g

items.title: UK taxpayers held more than £1tn in offshore tax havens, latest HMRC data shows
items.content:
Figures show recent 10% rise in total held in financial centres such as Jersey and Panama, raising fears over cost to public purse
The amount of money UK taxpayers hold in offshore accounts in tax havens has exceeded £1tn for the first time, raising concerns about potential losses to the public purse.
HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) data, obtained by the TaxWatch thinktank through freedom of information requests, shows between 2022 and 2024 the value of balances held offshore in tax havens increased by 10%. These were the latest available figures.

items.title: Why is Turkey warning of an Israeli military operation in Syria?
items.content:
Why is Turkey warning of an Israeli military operation in Syria?
Submitted by
Reem Aouir
on
Sun, 11/22/2026 - 13:21
FM Hakan Fidan says Israel is flying weapons to an armed Druze group in southern Syria every week to provoke the Syrian army, and that Ankara has warned Washington
A man hangs a poster of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu beside a Druze flag in Majdal Shams, Israeli-annexed Golan Heights, 17 October 2026 (Jalaa Marey/AFP)
Off
Turkey
's foreign minister has warned that
Israel
could launch a military operation in
Syria
, accusing it of backing a faction within the country's Druze community in an attempt to provoke the Syrian army and create a pretext for intervention.
Hakan Fidan made the remarks in a televised interview with Turkish broadcaster TGRT Haber on Saturday, saying Ankara had raised the possibility with regional allies, as well as US and European officials.
"There is a scenario in which the Israeli army uses this as a pretext to launch an operation against Syria," Fidan said.
The Turkish foreign minister also alleged that Israel was supporting one of three major factions within Syria's Druze community, supplying it with weapons and ammunition by helicopter on a weekly basis.
“In southern Syria, as you know, there are Druze. These Druze are divided into three major tribes within Syria. Two of these are genuinely on the side of the Syrian government and are anti-Israel. But one of them is supported by Israel.”
He claimed the faction was seeking to provoke Syrian government forces, potentially giving Israel justification to intervene militarily.
Omer Ozkizilcik, a non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, described Ankara’s warning as a precautionary move.
“Turkey's public warning aims at preventing Israel from doing something stupid in southern Syria before Israel actually does it,” he told Middle East Eye.
Fidan’s warning comes amid continued Israeli military activity in southern Syria and unresolved tensions between Damascus and Druze armed groups in the southern province of Sweida.
Sweida, the Druze-majority province in southern Syria, has been run as a de facto area under the spiritual leader Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, who has publicly aligned himself with Israel.
Most of its armed factions are grouped under the Sweida National Guard, a coalition of Druze militias backed by Israel and allied with al-Hijri.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan says Israel is supplying a Druze faction in southern Syria with weapons and ammunition by helicopter every week, seeking to provoke the Syrian army. Fidan warned that Israel intends to use these provocations as a pretext to launch a military operation and push further into Syrian territory. He said two of Syria’s three major Druze tribal groups support the Syrian government and oppose Israel, while the third is backed by Tel Aviv.
— Middle East Eye (@MiddleEastEye)
November 22, 2026
In July, al-Hijri suggested that Sweida could be integrated into Israel to preserve its autonomy.
Last month, The National reported, citing unnamed sources, that Israeli helicopters had dropped surveillance, radar and other equipment inside Sweida.
Flying over the Yarmouk River basin and villages in Deraa on the way to Sweida, sniper rifles and night-vision systems had also reached the National Guard.
A senior Syrian government official also told The Jerusalem Post in October that an Israeli helicopter had landed in Sweida and delivered significant quantities of weapons and ammunition.
Ozkizilcik also pointed to reports of Israeli helicopters arriving in Sweida and senior Israeli Druze military commanders visiting the province and meeting relatives, describing them as indications that tensions could be building.
"There is something potentially growing, but it's too early to clearly assess," he said.
'Destabilising neighbours'
Last week, the UN's deputy special envoy for Syria, Claudio Cordone, told the Security Council that Damascus had deployed additional forces to Sweida amid reports of continued Israeli support for local armed actors.
He said the province "remains in a tense security and political stalemate".
Supporters of Druze faction raise Israeli flags in Sweida on 7 October anniversary
Read More »
Fidan's remarks came days after he hosted his Syrian counterpart, Asaad al-Shaibani, in Ankara, where he called on Israel to halt its attacks in southern Syria and base its security arrangements on the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement.
"The security of any state cannot be built upon the destabilisation of its neighbours," Fidan said at the joint press conference on Tuesday.
Ozkizilcik described Ankara's warning as a precautionary move intended to deter Israel from launching an operation in southern Syria.
"Turkey is trying to raise awareness and prevent it from happening," he said.
Ankara is a close ally of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa's government.
In August, Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur airbase, about 70km from the Turkish border, later saying Damascus had been preparing to let Turkey deploy radar and air-defence systems operated by Turkish personnel there.
US envoy Tom Barrack later said the strike had been intended to bait Ankara.
“If Israel launched a major military ground offensive in southern Syria, this would open Pandora’s box for all kinds of military escalation,” Ozkizilcik told MEE.
Why is Syria considering joining the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact?
Read More »
He said such an offensive could turn into a wider confrontation involving Turkey, even if Ankara was reluctant to deploy its own troops directly.
"I do not see a scenario in which Turkey would not be involved in a military escalation against Israel," he said.
He added that Ankara would likely support the Syrian army and coordinate with Arab allies.
“It would be a disaster for Israel militarily, and also politically and diplomatically,” he said.
Ozkizilcik said the risk of Israeli escalation in Syria should also be viewed against the backdrop of Benjamin Netanyahu’s domestic political uncertainty, arguing that the Israeli prime minister had previously used military action to improve his electoral prospects.
“If he cannot go to war again against Iran due to American obstacles, the most likely area for him to launch a new war might be Syria,” he said.
In April, Fidan also stated that Israel was holding back from some actions in Syria because of the war on Iran, but had not abandoned them.
"Later, when the time comes, it may want to act," he said at the time.
'Israel first' vs 'America first'
During the interview, Fidan also shed light on
Gaza
and accused Israel of blocking thousands of container homes that Turkey had prepared for Gaza.
He said Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had ordered that the units, which Turkey used to house survivors of the 2023 earthquakes, be sent to the enclave.
"Israel is not allowing the containers to enter Gaza on the grounds that they are made of metal," Fidan said.
'Will throw keys back to UN': Trump-appointed Board of Peace adviser says Israel blocking efforts
Read More »
Israel claimed Hamas could use the metal to manufacture weapons, he added.
Fidan also described an ongoing "hidden struggle" in the
United States
between forces that put "Israel first" and those that put "America first".
He said US policy in the Middle East had for decades often served Israeli interests more than American ones, and that Netanyahu's policies had harmed Trump.
"Trump, who boasted of being a man who makes peace, seemed to have become a president who enters wars instead of achieving peace, and who fights on behalf of Israel," Fidan said.
He added that a growing current in the US was rejecting military intervention, and that public hostility towards Israel was rising.
Fidan also defended Turkey's role in the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed with
Saudi Arabia
and
Pakistan
in August, which commits each member to treat an attack on one as an attack on all three.
He said Ankara was giving Riyadh the defence support it needed, but accused critics in Turkey of exaggerating the pact.
He dismissed warnings in Turkey that soldiers would die in
Yemen's
desert, saying that unlike a century ago, when Yemen was Ottoman territory, it was now an independent state.
He also noted that Turkey had sent troops to Afghanistan as part of
Nato
without facing similar criticism.
"Why was there no problem when it concerned Nato, while there is a problem when it concerns a regional defence alliance in an Islamic region?" he said.

items.title: Netanyahu, Eisenkot parties end talks without deal on forming Israel govt
items.content:
The parties of caretaker Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot concluded a new round of talks on Sunday without reaching an agreement on a possible coalition government, which would require concessions from both sides.
Delegations from Eisenkot's Yashar party and Netanyahu's Likud met for four hours at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, following a first round of discussions last Sunday.

items.title: Netanyahu and Eisenkot parties resume talks to form Israel govt
items.content:
The parties of caretaker Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot launched a new round of talks on Sunday over whether to form a coalition government, with Netanyahu's party insisting on keeping his main policies.
Delegations from Eisenkot's Yashar party and Netanyahu's Likud began their confab at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, an AFP journalist on the scene said, following a first round of talks last Sunday.

items.title: Israel: Eisenkot and Netanyahu parties meet again for unity government talks
items.content:
Israel: Eisenkot and Netanyahu parties meet again for unity government talks
Representatives from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and the party of his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, met on Sunday to discuss forming a unity government, Haaretz is
reporting
.
The meeting follows earlier talks last Sunday after nearly a month of deadlock in the Israeli Knesset since October's election, which saw no party gain an overall majority. Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have so far failed to negotiate a viable coalition government alongside smaller parties.
Absent from Sunday's meeting were representatives of Naftali Bennett's Together party, which received the third-largest vote share and attended the previous round of talks.

items.title: Experts say ‘trusted messengers’ critical as Amish grapple with measles outbreak
items.content:
Unfolding crisis shows importance of ‘human connections’ over the long term – especially in under-vaccinated areas
Tristan Sharratt, a family nurse practitioner and public health researcher, began serving an Amish community in central New York almost inadvertently. A friend told an Amish neighbor that Sharratt was accepting new patients and was a good, solid guy. Word spread quickly, and now Sharratt sees many members of the community, which numbers in the hundreds.
He is what is called a “trusted messenger” – someone who understands a community and has earned their respect. Other trusted messengers can be neighbors, co-workers, customers, midwives, or people who work as long-distance drivers for the Amish. Connecting with such people will be crucial for ending the measles outbreak and preventing future crises.

items.title: Australia urged to wean off imported fossil fuels amid global supply shocks
items.content:
Grattan Institute report calls on government to seize opportunity to cap diesel tax credits, introduce EV subsidies for less wealthy and build ‘clean’ refineries
Get our
daily political email
,
free app
or
daily news podcast
Capping lucrative diesel tax handouts to big business, building new “clean” refineries and targeting electric vehicle subsidies to less wealthy people could save Australians thousands of dollars in fuel per year, according to a major new report calling on the government to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels.
The Grattan Institute has warned Australia imports too much of its fuel and that the country must brace for more global supply shocks – like those from the war in Iran. Under a plan already attracting criticism from business groups, Grattan urged diesel handouts to mining and primary industries be curbed in favour of incentives for electric trucks and a huge expansion of the EV charging network.

items.title: COP31 climate talks set to collapse without political deal
items.content:
ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 22 (Reuters) - UN climate talks in Turkey looked set to collapse without a political agreement after COP31 summit president Murat Kurum said there would be no new draft of the deal.
Earlier, multiple countries and negotiating blocs said they could not accept the version of the text put before them.
"There will be no new text from now on. We will not be carrying out work on a new text in an environment where there is no consensus," Kurum said.
(Reporting by Tuvan Gumrukcu, writing by William James)

items.title: Climate deal collapses in chaotic end to COP31
items.content:
The COP31 climate talks ended in failure Sunday as a contentious deal collapsed over fossil fuels and the summit stretched into record overtime in Turkey.
The final agreement was dramatically rejected in a chaotic finale to a UN climate summit which ran two days over schedule, underscoring the strains on diplomacy in an increasingly fractured world.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, who urged nations to send fossil fuels "the way of the dinosaurs" during a fiery appearance at COP31, expressed deep dismay as the talks broke down.

items.title: COP31 fails to agree climate deal in chaotic finale
items.content:
The COP31 climate talks headed for a historic defeat Sunday after the EU and other countries refused to endorse a pact that omitted fossil fuels as the summit lurched into record overtime in Turkey.
The main deal was rejected by a host of nations 44 hours after the summit's official close in a chaotic COP31 finale in the Turkish city of Antalya.

items.title: Saudi Arabia, Qatar join condemnation of Iran attack on Bahrain
items.content:
Saudi Arabia, Qatar join condemnation of Iran attack on Bahrain
Saudi Arabia and Qatar have joined the UAE in condemning Iran's attack on Bahrain earlier on Sunday.
In a statement
posted
on X, Qatar's foreign ministry expressed its "categorical rejection of attacks on economic facilities, civilian objects and civilians, and affirms that the continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that threatens the region’s security and stability”.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, said it "affirms its full solidarity with Bahrain in all measures it takes to protect its security and stability", accusing Tehran of "undermining regional security and stability”.
Iran attacked US military bases in both Qatar and Saudi Arabia, along with Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE, Oman, Iraq and Jordan throughout the first months of the war, which began in late February. But such attacks have lulled since April amid ceasefire negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
#Statement | The Foreign Ministry expresses the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia’s condemnation and denunciation, in the strongest terms, of the heinous Iranian attacks on a civilian industrial facility in the brotherly Kingdom of Bahrain. items.title: The life, death and improbable rebirth of LA’s most beloved diner
items.content:
For decades, it served pancakes, hash browns and steaks to hungry Angelenos. Then came closure, and a city mourned – but now the Original Pantry is back
Sometimes, an old-school American diner is just a diner. And sometimes, like the Original Pantry in downtown Los Angeles, it feels like the heart and soul of a city, a bellwether of good times and bad.
For decades it was famous for never closing. Located in a low-slung shotgun building on a busy corner, it fed politicians, movie stars, students, criminals and street bums around the clock, seven days a week. The doors had no locks, because the place had no need for them. The portions were huge, the prices dirt cheap, and many of the servers, in bow ties and white shirts, looked like extras from a Harold Lloyd two-reeler.

items.title: Cop31 ends in failure as countries reject climate deal over fossil fuels
items.content:
Cop31 ends in failure as countries reject climate deal over fossil fuels
The United Nations climate summit in Turkey became the longest-ever UN climate conference on Sunday as negotiations over a final agreement descended into deadlock, with the European Union and several other countries formally rejecting the proposed text.
The talks in Antalya, known as Cop31, continued more than 44 hours beyond their scheduled Friday conclusion, surpassing the previous record set by Cop25 in Madrid in 2019.
The latest draft, presented by the Turkish and Australian presidencies in an attempt to bridge divisions between countries, failed to secure consensus over its omission of explicit references to fossil fuels and disagreements over climate finance.
At the closing plenary, Cop31 President Murat Kurum acknowledged that countries had failed to agree on the proposed document.
“We have done our utmost. Ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” Kurum said.
This is a developing story. We'll bring more updates shortly.

items.title: 'Deserved to fail': Cop31 ends in failure as countries reject deal over fossil fuels
items.content:
'Deserved to fail': Cop31 ends in failure as countries reject deal over fossil fuels
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Sun, 11/22/2026 - 12:38
European Union, Panama and other countries reject the final proposal over its failure to explicitly address fossil fuels
Cop31 President and Turkey's Minister of Environment Murat Kurum attends a session of the UN Climate Change Conference (Cop31) in Antalya on 22 November 2026 (AFP)
Off
The Cop31 climate summit in Turkey ended without agreement after the European Union and several countries rejected a proposed deal that failed to explicitly address fossil fuels and provide stronger financial support to developing nations.
Cop31 President Murat Kurum said that the negotiations had failed to secure consensus, adding that the proposed decisions had not been adopted.
"It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted," he told the closing plenary.
"We have done our utmost. Ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum such as a 'take it or leave it' demand."
The European Union, the Marshall Islands, Panama, Norway and Vanuatu were among those that formally objected to the proposed Antalya Pact.
The talks had been scheduled to end on Friday but continued until Sunday, as negotiators tried to resolve disagreements over the proposed agreement.
The breakdown followed more than two weeks of negotiations, making the summit the longest in the history of the UN climate conference process.
Cop31 draft agreement ‘the worst ever', campaigners warn
Read More »
Ireland's Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, formally rejected the Antalya Pact, saying it failed to meet the urgency of the climate crisis.
"We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required… that does not even mention fossil fuels," he said.
The dispute centred on the omission of an explicit reference to transitioning away from coal, oil and gas, despite the commitment made by countries at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023.
The latest draft referred to earlier decisions, including the Dubai agreement, but did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.
It also retained provisions on carbon capture and storage, a technology promoted by some oil-producing countries but criticised by environmental groups as a potential means of prolonging fossil fuel production.
'Moves us backwards'
The United Kingdom criticised the proposed agreement. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the summit had failed to build the consensus required for meaningful climate action.
"This Cop sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with ever more urgency to address it.
"The moment required bold ambition, and we have been working tirelessly to try to build consensus. It is immensely disappointing we have been unable to do so," she said.
Greta Thunberg at COP: Turkish energy shipments 'directly fuelling the genocide of Palestine'
Read More »
The UK described the text as a setback, saying: "It moves us backwards; it is the lowest common denominator when it should have been uniting us in action."
Panama also formally rejected the agreement, saying the text failed to address its demands.
"What we cannot accept is that we are asked to drop our stance because the atmosphere does not negotiate, the planet does not negotiate," the representative said.
The Republic of the Marshall Islands also rejected the proposed agreement, warning that it threatened the security of vulnerable island nations.
"We will not be forced to accept false solutions. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security," its representative said.
"Our needs are so great, but the gap keeps growing. People are dying, the seas are rising."
Norway also joined the objections, while Germany had earlier indicated that it would not accept the draft in its existing form.
'Deserved to fail'
Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, told Middle East Eye that the proposed agreement had failed on four critical fronts: fossil fuels, climate finance, adaptation and loss and damage.
Singh said a reference to the Cop28 outcome was insufficient, arguing that the Dubai agreement had gone further by calling for a transition away from fossil fuels.
Weapon of distraction: How Israel uses greenwashing to mask its climate crimes
Read More »
“A mere reference to the Cop28 outcome was never going to be enough. Three years ago in Dubai, we got a far better text that called for a transition away from fossil fuels. This rejection shows the world will not accept going backwards," he said.
Singh, who is a global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, accused wealthy countries of resisting efforts to establish measurable financial commitments under the Paris Agreement.
“Rich countries were reminded of the Paris Agreement provision that says they must pay, but they forced the deletion of every number that would show whether they have.
"They even erased the word 'debt' from a finance decision, while countries across Asia and Africa spend more on debt repayments than on protecting their people. That is why this text deserved to fail,” he told MEE.
Singh said the proposed outcome also failed to provide adequate support for adaptation, which he described as a matter of survival for vulnerable communities.
“The Adaptation Fund, which delivers money directly to frontline communities, raised barely $50m here against a target of $300m a year. The text's response was to 'encourage contributions', with no amount, no deadline and no country named," he said.
"With the $120bn figure deleted and the tripling pathway pushed to 2027, the message to the world's most vulnerable was clear: you're on your own."

items.title: 'Jewish terrorism in every sense': Eisenkot blames Smotrich and Ben Gvir for settler attacks
items.content:
'Jewish terrorism in every sense': Eisenkot blames Smotrich and Ben Gvir for settler attacks
Israeli politician Gadi Eisenkot has condemned a series of arson attacks by settlers in the occupied West Bank as "Jewish terrorism", accusing far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir of fuelling violence against Palestinians.
Settlers attacked the villages of Deir al-Sudan, Deir Abu Mashal and Kafr Malik, near Ramallah, overnight between Saturday and Sunday, setting fire to Palestinian-owned vehicles and spraying racist graffiti on homes, according to Palestinian media reports.
Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, described the attacks as "Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word" and called on the government and security establishment to take tougher action against violent settlers.
"The acts of sabotage carried out by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermine regional stability, endanger lives and seriously harm Israel's national security and foreign relations," he wrote on X.
Eisenkot was tasked with forming Israel's next government on 8 November by President Isaac Herzog.
He accused National Security Minister Ben Gvir and Finance Minister Smotrich of bringing the West Bank "to the brink of unchecked anarchy".
"This reality is not inevitable," he said, describing it as the consequence of poor leadership.
He said authorities should use all available measures, including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, to stop the perpetrators.

Yair Lapid, another opposition politician, also condemned the attacks,
describing
them as "terrorism" resulting from government negligence.
"Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence on the part of the Israeli government," Lapid said.
"By remaining silent, government ministers are deliberately encouraging these pogroms," he added.
"When we form a government, we will tackle this terrorism and restore governance, law and order."
The Palestinian news agency Wafa reported that 12 vehicles were set on fire across the three Palestinian villages.
Israeli police said they had opened investigations into arson, vandalism and property damage.
Settler violence displacing Palestinians
The latest attacks come amid a sustained escalation in settler violence across the occupied West Bank, where Palestinian communities have faced assaults, arson, property destruction, restrictions on access to farmland and the expansion of settlement outposts.
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha)
recorded
40 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage across 30 Palestinian communities between 10 and 16 November.
Palestinian families brace for expulsion as settlers erect outpost near West Bank village
Read More »
The attacks left 38 Palestinians injured and displaced 68 people, including 31 children.
Ocha also recorded 428 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage during the 2026 olive harvest season between 1 September and 16 November.
The incidents have disrupted farmers' access to their land and damaged agricultural property and livelihoods.
In October, the UN agency
recorded
467 settler attacks, the highest monthly figure since it began documenting such incidents in 2006.
Ocha said settler violence and access restrictions had
displaced
about 6,800 Palestinians, including more than 3,200 children, across 137 communities since January 2023.
In 2026 alone, 2,894 Palestinians had been displaced by such violence. The attacks have also been linked to the expansion of settlement outposts and the gradual loss of Palestinian access to land.
According to Israeli settlement watchdog Peace Now, settlers had
taken control
of more than 100,000 dunams (10,000 hectares) of land in Areas A and B, with violence and threats used to restrict Palestinian access and, in some cases, pressure families to leave their homes.

items.title: They went out to celebrate at a Memphis bar. Then, ICE descended
items.content:
More than 120 people in the Tennessee city were detained in one of the largest single-day ICE raids in the US in 2026
The date 1 September, or 9/01 Day, is a festive day for Memphians. The date mirrors the city’s 901 area code, and gives residents a reason to come together to celebrate the city and the people who love it. When 9/01 Day falls on a weekday, as it did this year, the celebration starts the weekend prior, extending the festivities. Groups across the city hosted celebrations featuring food vendors, DJs, musicians and members of the
Memphis Grizzlies
, the local
NBA
team, while dozens of local businesses offered $9.01-themed specials.
But for the families of 121 people, this past 1 September will be remembered for a different reason – just days prior, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers detained their friends and relatives, conducting one of the largest single-day raids in the country this year, and the
largest known one in Memphis
.

items.title: Araghchi talks down Qatari visit
items.content:
Araghchi talks down Qatari visit
Iranian
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has talked down the significance of a Qatari delegation's visit to Tehran on Friday.
“Such a trip is not unusual at all. Intermediaries are constantly in contact with Iran and the
US
, holding meetings with both sides and conveying proposals between them,” Araghchi told reporters in Tehran on Sunday.
Qatar
, which has sought to mediate between the US and Iran throughout the conflict, has not commented on the talks.

items.title: UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’
items.content:
Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long
British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products.
The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to
benefit Britain’s food exporters
and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks.

items.title: Countries react as COP31 climate talks collapse
items.content:
ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 22 (Reuters) - The COP31 conference in Turkey ended in collapse on Sunday after countries failed to agree an overarching political deal on how to tackle climate change.
Below are reactions from delegates:
ANTONIO GUTERRES, UNITED NATIONS SECRETARY GENERAL
"I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands."

items.title: UAE condemns Iranian attack on Bahrain
items.content:
UAE condemns Iranian attack on Bahrain
The UAE has condemned the Iranian attacks on Bahrain as a “flagrant violation” of the Gulf state's sovereignty.
In a statement, Abu Dhabi reiterated “the UAE’s full solidarity with the sisterly kingdom of Bahrain and its support for all measures taken to safeguard its security and stability”.
Earlier on Sunday, Bahrain’s interior ministry said Iran attacked a civilian industrial facility near its capital, Manama. Iran said that the strike targeted air defence systems at two US military bases.

items.title: How Europe’s green hydrogen ambitions could keep Tunisia’s worst polluter alive
items.content:
How Europe’s green hydrogen ambitions could keep Tunisia’s worst polluter alive
Submitted by
Francesco Torri
on
Tue, 11/17/2026 - 11:13
A German-backed plan sold as a clean energy transition is seen by many Tunisians as a lifeline for a heavily polluting phosphate industry
Smoke billows from the chimney of a section of the state-run phosphate processing plant in the southern city of Gabes on 31 October 2025 (Fethi Belaid/AFP)
Off
As
Tunisia
’s green hydrogen strategy is being promoted as a cornerstone of Europe’s clean energy transition, residents in the southern city of Gabes argue it could instead extend the life of one of the country’s most polluting industrial complexes while increasing pressure on scarce resources.
On 21 October 2025, around 100,000 people
marched
through Gabes in one of the largest environmental
protests
North Africa
has seen in years. Demonstrators demanded the closure of the Groupe Chimique Tunisien (GCT), the state-owned phosphate complex that has polluted the city’s air and sea for decades.
Residents also mobilised against plans to decarbonise the GCT and turn it into a green hydrogen hub supplying Europe. Critics describe the project as a form of “green colonialism”, saying Tunisia would bear the environmental costs while Europe reaps most of the benefits.
Germany, which expects to import
50 to 70 percent
of its hydrogen demand by 2030, has been the leading force behind Tunisia’s National Green Hydrogen Strategy,
published
in July 2024. Berlin financed the strategy and provided the technical expertise behind its design through GIZ’s
H2Vert.TUN
project.
As the strategy itself states, Tunisia aims to produce 8.3 million tonnes of green hydrogen annually by 2050. Of that total, only around 2 million tonnes would remain in the country. The strategy identifies the production of green ammonia at the GCT’s Gabes complex as the main and earliest domestic use planned for green hydrogen in Tunisia, while most of the remaining output would be exported to Europe.
Green hydrogen would replace the fossil hydrogen the GCT uses to produce ammonia for fertilisers and reduce its carbon emissions. But this “decarbonisation” would do nothing to address the plant’s other major sources of pollution, including sulphur dioxide, fluorides and phosphogypsum, which have contaminated the environment for decades and continue to
make Gabes’ residents sick.
The hydrogen is expected to be exported to Europe through the
EU-backed
SoutH2 Corridor
. In parallel, Brussels
pledged
€35.4m ($38.9m) for Tunisia’s renewable energy infrastructure, while
agreements
signed with energy multinationals envisaged €120bn in private investment.
Yet little progress has followed.
“Everybody is waiting for something to develop,” Edward Koenen, head of finance and sales at ABO Energy, one of the companies that signed a memorandum of understanding, told Middle East Eye.
“The Tunisian government said they are not that interested in constructing anything, because there is no market for green hydrogen.”
Officially, Tunis has not changed course. On 1 October, it reaffirmed its commitment to the SoutH2 pipeline project by signing the
Algiers Ministerial Declaration
, but nothing has progressed beyond paper.
As the high costs associated with green hydrogen have become clearer, what some analysts once described as Europe’s “hydrogen hype” has begun to fade. In September 2025, the International Energy Agency cut its
2030 forecast
for low-emissions hydrogen production by a quarter.
No to ‘green facade’
However, according to Saber Ammar, a Tunisian activist and researcher at the Tunisian think tank Transnational Institute, there is another element behind Tunisia’s stall on its green hydrogen strategy: the opposition of Gabes’ residents and Tunisian civil society.
Opponents argue that the projects would primarily benefit European consumers while entrenching an industrial model that many residents of Gabes want dismantled.
“There was a coalition between the trade union, the social movement, the environmental justice movement, and we created some sort of an anti-green hydrogen front,” Saber told MEE.
‘Last year, starting from September, hundreds of people went to the hospital due to suffocation caused by the gases emitted by the industry’
- Islem Zrelli, member of Stop Pollution
One of the key components in this coalition is “Stop Pollution”, an environmental movement born in 2012 in Gabes to oppose the severe pollution and health impacts caused by the GCT.
Kheireddine Debia, one of Stop Pollution’s leaders, told MEE that what activists want "is to shut down the industrial complex, not to give it a green facade".
Debia
received
a six-month suspended sentence last month for protesting against the GCT, while nine other activists were
handed
prison terms of up to a year as part of a broader
crackdown
on dissent since President Kais Saied’s
power grab
in 2021.
Islem Zrelli, a young member of Stop Pollution, believes the GCT has already done too much damage. Last year’s protests erupted after more than 120 residents were hospitalised following severe gas leaks.
“Last year, starting from September, hundreds of people went to the hospital due to suffocation caused by the gases emitted by the industry,” he told MEE. “Many of them were kids and students from Chatt Essalem, my neighbourhood.”
Tunisia: Thousands protest in Gabes against chemical plant pollution
Read More »
The GCT’s phosphate processing and fertiliser production have caused long-term health problems among the population, including chronic respiratory illnesses. Its radioactive waste product,
phosphogypsum
, has been linked to higher cancer rates and has polluted the Gulf of Gabes, harming marine life and contaminating waters that residents rely on for their livelihoods and food.
In 2017, thanks to Stop Pollution’s mobilisation and civil society pressure, the government
promised
to dismantle the phosphate unit.
However, on 5 March 2025, a restricted ministerial council chaired by Prime Minister Kamel Maddouri
reversed course
. It removed phosphogypsum from Tunisia’s list of hazardous wastes, despite an estimated 70 million tonnes of the material having been dumped by the plant into the Mediterranean over the previous 25 years.
The controversial move is part of a 2025-2030 plan to
expand
phosphate production from under three million to 14 million tonnes a year. The council also approved the creation of pilot green ammonia units in Gabes, envisaged as the cornerstone of Tunisia’s domestic green hydrogen industry and a key component of the export-oriented hydrogen economy outlined in the German-backed national strategy.
For the people of Gabes, this means more phosphogypsum in the sea and higher emissions of toxic gases into the air, including ammonia, which a GCT audit
found
to be already exceeding permitted levels in 2025.
Green extractivism
Critics say Tunisia’s green hydrogen strategy could also carry significant social and economic costs.
“The problem is that green hydrogen needs fresh water, and Tunisia doesn’t have any fresh water,” Fadhel Kaboub, associate professor of economics at Denison University and president of the Global Institute for Sustainable Prosperity, told MEE.
“So the solution is desalination, and desalination plants produce the salt brine, which is chemically toxic for sea life, that is dumped usually in the ocean. It kills the blue economy.”
‘It is reminiscent of the fossil fuel system. And with green hydrogen, we risk reproducing that model, with more foreign debt’
- Hanen Keskes, Greenpeace MENA
The worsening water stress that environmentalists have warned about for years has already become a reality in Tunisia. This year, the country faced its
hottest summer on record
, with power cuts that stopped the water pumps and left towns without water for days, prompting protests across the country.
According to the Transnational Institute’s
analysis
of the strategy, exporting six million tonnes of green hydrogen would also require more than 90 gigawatts of solar and wind capacity covering 500,000 hectares, about 3 percent of Tunisia and roughly twice the area of Greater Tunis.
Most of it would be
concentrated
in a planned “hydrogen valley” in southern Tunisia, much of it on communal land used by local communities for herding and small-scale farming. The strategy, however, offers few details on how such land would be secured.
Since 2016, Tunisia has
loosened land laws
to open agricultural and collective land to energy investors. In villages such as Segdoud, collective land has already been
appropriated
by the state for solar projects without compensation, according to residents and rights advocates.
Moreover, while the
strategy
promises more than 400,000 jobs by 2050, a 2021
study
commissioned by GIZ warned that producing hydrogen with imported technology and exporting it as a raw material “would create limited jobs and value in Tunisia”. The study added that most of the jobs created would be temporary, tied to the construction of solar and wind projects.
Green hydrogen: The EU's new resource grab in North Africa
Read More »
Hamza Hamouchene, a founding member of the Environmental Justice North Africa (EJNA) network and programme coordinator at the Transnational Institute, argues that the strategy risks reproducing an extractivist economic model, where Europe profits from North Africa’s minimally processed resources while local communities see few lasting gains.
“Europe and its companies, what we call the Global North, want to continue to get their cheap natural resources, including green electricity and green hydrogen,” he told MEE. “Yet these projects end up not creating long-term, sustainable, good jobs for local populations.”
Officials estimate that producing every million tonnes of green hydrogen would
require
$25bn in investment, a cost they acknowledge Tunisia cannot bear alone. Critics warn that the strategy could lock the country into a new cycle of foreign debt, with public financing used to reduce risks for foreign investors.
“This is the built-in problem with extractivism, including green extractivism,” Hanen Keskes, political campaign lead at Greenpeace MENA, told MEE.
“You de-risk the European corporations through government loans, while just exporting raw, very depletable resources. It is reminiscent of the fossil fuel system. And with green hydrogen, we risk reproducing that model, with more foreign debt.”
Inside Tunisia
Achref Chibani
Jasper Humpert
Gabes, Tunisia

•
Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds
British businesses run by long-serving directors of the Bank of England profited from “brutal” enslavement in Cuba for decades after slavery’s abolition in the British empire, according to research.
Men and boys were enslaved in prison conditions at the El Cobre copper ore mine near Santiago de Cuba, which supplied British firms during the Industrial Revolution, the historian Chris Evans has found.

items.title: Morning update
items.content:
Morning update
Good Morning Middle East Eye readers,
If you are just joining us, here are key developments from across the region and beyond:
*Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says its forces attacked two US bases in Bahrain; Manama says strikes hit civilian industrial facility.
*The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by Yemen's Houthis towards Saudi Arabia's western region.
*Two Palestinians injured in an Israeli strike on Gaza succumb as territory's health ministry says death toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” rises to 1,661.
*Israeli settlers torched Palestinian-owned vehicles and spray-painted alleged racist graffiti on Palestinian homes in several West Bank villages.
*The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) has urged Germany to arrest an Israeli soldier, Almog Keisi, who has been sighted in Luneburg this week, accusing him of war crimes, crimes against humanity and acts of genocide in Gaza.
*Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said Israel is blocking thousands of container homes destined for Gaza, adding that Israeli authorities argue Hamas could use the metal structures  for manufacturing weapons.
*Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said that his country was engaged in a "silent war that is far more difficult than the one in which missiles are launched and destruction is inflicted".
*Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has accused Iran of meddling in Lebanon's affairs through Hezbollah's weapons and also demanded Israel withdraw from the country's south.
*Pro-Israel US Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries has pledged to advance legislation targeting Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank within the first 100 days of the new Congress.

items.title: Israeli settlers torch vehicles in West Bank, paint 'racist' graffiti on homes
items.content:
Israeli settlers torch vehicles in West Bank, paint 'racist' graffiti on homes
Israeli settlers set fire to 12 Palestinian-owned vehicles and spray-painted racist graffiti during attacks on three villages in Ramallah and al-Bireh in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian media reported.
Local sources told Wafa that a group of settlers attacked the village of Kafr Malik, east of Ramallah, setting fire to seven vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on the walls of some homes.
In a separate attack, colonists raided the town of Deir Abu Mash'al, northwest of Ramallah, setting fire to three vehicles and spraying racist graffiti before fleeing the area.
In Deir al-Sudan, north of Ramallah, colonists set fire to two vehicles belonging to two Palestinian citizens, causing extensive material damage.
Israeli police, according to Haaretz, said they had opened an investigation into arson, graffiti and property damage at four sites in the West Bank.
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot condemned the attacks, calling them "Jewish terrorism" and warning that extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes were pushing the West Bank toward "anarchy."
Israeli settler militias set fire to several Palestinian vehicles in the village of Kafr Malik, east of Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, in the early hours of Sunday. https://t.co/Rvh60XZpXN

An explosion struck an ammunition depot inside a naval base in Libya's eastern port city of Benghazi on Sunday morning, local emergency authorities said, according to Al-Masar TV, a news channel.
The authorities have not disclosed the cause of the explosion or whether it caused any casualty. Emergency response teams were deployed to the military facility following the blast to contain the resulting fire.

items.title: Fire at confectionery factory in Indonesia leaves at least three dead and dozens missing
items.content:
Relatives of the missing victims flocked to the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones
A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36 remaining missing, an Indonesian rescue official says.
Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex. Photos and videos shared by rescuers show officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims on Sunday, with small fires still burning in some spots.

items.title: IRGC chief says Iran's air space 'red line' for armed forces
items.content:
IRGC chief says Iran's air space 'red line' for armed forces
Commander-in-Chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Major General Ahmad Vahidi has said that Iran’s airspace is a red line for the country's armed forces and any breach will be met with a "firm and decisive response", Mehr news agency reported.
On Saturday, Major General Vahidi visited Iran's underground missile city for the first time as the force unveiled a new dual-missile launcher.
During his visit, Vahidi said that "events unfolding for the enemy were only the beginning" and that "the enemy would witness humiliation and defeat and that truth would prevail over falsehood", according to Mehr.

items.title: مباشر: البحرين تتهم إيران باستهداف "منشأة صناعية مدنية" والتحالف بقيادة السعودية يتصدى لهجمات حوثية
items.content:
مباشر: البحرين تتهم إيران باستهداف "منشأة صناعية مدنية" والتحالف بقيادة السعودية يتصدى لهجمات حوثية
نشب حريق في منشأة صناعية بالبحرين جراء ضربة إيرانية السبت، وفق ما أعلنت المملكة التي استهدفتها أربعة هجومات منذ منتصف تشرين الثاني/نوفمبر، فيما تؤكّد طهران أنها تردّ على الضربات الأمريكية في ظلّ تصاعد حدّة النزاع في الشرق الأوسط. من جهته، أفاد ​التحالف الذي تقوده ​السعودية السبت بأنه اعترض ودمر ​صاروخا ‌باليستيا أطلقه الحوثيون باتجاه المنطقة ‌الغربية في المملكة، وسط تصاعد حدة التوتر بين السعودية والجماعة ​المتحالفة مع ‌إيران. تابعوا تغطيتنا المباشرة.

👈 اقرأ المزيد: https://f24.my/CIdR.g

items.title: Israeli puts 'Gaza mosque crescent finial' up for sale, rights group says
items.content:
Israeli puts 'Gaza mosque crescent finial' up for sale, rights group says
An Israeli rights group has shared an image of an Israeli offering for sale a purported crescent finial from a mosque in Gaza's Rafah crossing.
In a post on X, Mistaclim said "a pious Jew" trades "in loot, in the spoils of war".
"Offers for sale for 2,500 shekels the moon at the end of the central mosque in the Rafah crossing and boasts that he has proof," the post read.
"And perhaps the problem lies in the rotten Israeli society, where the destruction of a place of worship is an opportunity for 'pride in the living room'."
"עברי חסיד" סוחר בביזה, בשלל מלחמה. מציע למכירה ב- 2,500 ש"ח את "הירח בסוף של המסגד המרכזי במעבר רפיח", ומתגאה שיש לו הוכחות. ו​אולי הבעיה בחברה הישראלית הרקובה בה חורבן של מקום תפילה הוא אפשרות ל"גאווה בסלון". https://t.co/W8lyTA9FWq
— מסתכלים לכיבוש בעיניים (@Mistaclim)
November 21, 2026

items.title: Labour MPs sign up for leadership course to counter rightwing populism
items.content:
Course run by former No 10 advisers is funded by Gary Lubner, who has given more than £11m to Labour
More than 20 Labour MPs have signed up to a year-long leadership course helping them to counter rightwing populism and deal with hostility, run by two former No 10 advisers and ultimately funded by multimillionaire donor Gary Lubner.
The training courses worth about £9,600 are being led by Ruth Turner, who was Tony Blair’s director of government relations, and Peter Hyman, who has worked for Blair, Keir Starmer and Andy Burnham’s governments.

items.title: ‘Serious error of judgment’: outrage over military AI event at Berlin arts complex
items.content:
Kraftwerk Berlin, part of same development as techno club Tresor, transformed into ‘war room’ for arms firm event
With their cavernous post-industrial venues, teeth-grinding four-by-four beats and bouncers that look like Blade Runner extras, Berlin’s nightclubs trade on a reputation for bleakness. A recent event at one of the city’s most legendary clubland institutions, however, has proven too dystopian even for seasoned techno-heads.
On 11 November, the Kraftwerk Berlin arts complex had its central hall transformed into what visitors described as something resembling a war room, with maps and aerial footage projected on to concrete walls, drones hanging from the ceiling, and guards in flak jackets patrolling the premises with sniffer dogs.

items.title: Europe is entering a ‘supercycle’ of national elections. Their outcomes could shake the EU’s foundations
items.content:
As nationalist, Eurosceptic parties surge in four of the bloc’s biggest member states, the coming year’s polls could test its resilience like never before
In late 1998, Tony Blair was prime minister of Britain, Lionel Jospin was prime minister of France, and Gerhard Schröder had just been elected chancellor of Germany. The EU had 15 member states and pro-European, centre-left parties were in power – either alone or in coalitions – in all but two of them.
Brisk economic growth was lifting living standards. Eastward enlargement was under way. In Washington, Bill Clinton was pursuing the same brand of “third way” centrism as a middle path between free-market capitalism and traditional socialism. The EU felt like it had the tide of history behind it.

items.title: World Central Kitchen founder says three killed in Gaza strike 'not part of our team'
items.content:
World Central Kitchen founder says three killed in Gaza strike 'not part of our team'
The founder of the World Central Kitchen, Jose Andres, has said that the three people killed in an Israeli strike on a vehicle delivering food aid in Gaza, did not belong the organisation, nor did the vehicle.
In a post on X, Andres said, "Early reports linked them to World Central Kitchen. They were not part of our team, and it was not our vehicle. That's all we know."
"But here is what I do know. More than a year into a ceasefire, people in Gaza are still dying. Families are facing a fourth winter in tents," he added.
The Israeli army had earlier claimed in a post on X that it targeted three “Islamic Jihad terrorists” in a vehicle used to transport food and supplies to other group operatives in Gaza.
Andres added that a "ceasefire is not peace", calling upon leaders to work towards ending the conflict.
"To every leader with the power to change this, on every side: finish the work. End this war for good, so Palestinians and Israelis can live in safety, and so the people of Gaza can start to rebuild their homes, their schools, their kitchens," he said.
"Our teams, Gazans feeding Gazans, were cooking again today. They will be there tomorrow. A plate of food is hope. But it is not a future. Peace is."

items.title: South Korean minister quits after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams
items.content:
Choi Kyo-jin says he ‘failed to prepare adequately’ for entrance exams following last-minute scramble to tighten measures

items.title: Pro-Israel Hakeem Jeffries says he will push legislation targeting settler violence
items.content:
Pro-Israel Hakeem Jeffries says he will push legislation targeting settler violence
Pro-Israel US Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the first Black speaker of the House of Representatives next year, has pledged to advance legislation targeting Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank within the first 100 days of the new Congress.
In an interview with The New York Times, Jeffries said the West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act should be among the early legislative priorities, adding that he expected strong support for it within the House Democratic Caucus.
Jeffries also described the devastation inflicted on Palestinian civilians in Gaza as “unacceptable, unsustainable and un-American”, calling for increased humanitarian assistance, medical aid, housing support and access to clean water and air.
Asked whether he supported the proposed Block the Bombs and Stop the Settlements bills, which call for restricting arms sale to Israel and broader sanctions on settlement expansion, Jeffries said he had not taken a position.
On calls to halt US weapons exports used in regional conflicts, he said the current approach was “not sustainable” and needed to change.
More than a million people have signed a petition urging Democrats to reject Hakeem Jeffries as the next Speaker of the US House of Representative. An Economist/YouGov poll published last month found that Jeffries had just a 26 percent approval rating among registered voters.
Critics say that one reason Jeffries' popularity has taken a hit is that he is an avid supporter of Israel.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) ranks among his top campaign-financing contributors.
Jeffries said he expects strong support for the West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act. (AFP)

items.title: Turkey says Israel could use Druze support to launch Syria operation
items.content:
Turkey says Israel could use Druze support to launch Syria operation
Israeli could use its support of the Druze to launch an operation in Syria, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said, warning that such an attack could lead to a wider conflict in the region.
In an interview with Turkish media, Fidan said Israel is providing military equipment and support to a Druze tribe in Syria, and may use that support to provoke the Syrian army and launch an attack.
Fidan said Turkey has discussed such the possibility of this operation with European and American officials.
The violence last year in Druze-majority Sweida - which began with clashes between Druze factions and Bedouin fighters in the southern province - left more than 2,000 people dead, including 789 Druze civilians, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights.
The Sweida violence also saw Israel launching air strikes in the province as well as in the capital Damascus, nominally in support of the Druze minority. In August, it struck a Syrian airbase where it said Turkey was planning to deploy forces.

Turkish foreign minister says Iran war fallout threatening global markets
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said the economic burden brought by the US-Israel war is getting harder for many countries, while emphasising a ceasefire was needed to reverse global financial crises.
Speaking to Turkish broadcaster TGRT Haber on Saturday, Fidan warned that the fallout from the conflict is threatening international markets.
“It is heading toward having very destructive effects,” he said.
Fidan said diplomatic efforts to re-open the Strait of Hormuz remain active, even though the process appears to be deadlocked, citing his recent discussion with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani.
He also said that Ankara was keeping the humanitarian crisis in Gaza on the global radar permanently despite other international crises.
"In every speech, every initiative, and every platform wherever it may be, the Gaza issue is one we have not, and will not, allow to be forgotten," Fidan said.

items.title: Israeli occupation, Iranian interference threat to Lebanese sovereignty, Aoun says
items.content:
Israeli occupation, Iranian interference threat to Lebanese sovereignty, Aoun says
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has accused Iran of meddling in Lebanon's affairs through Hezbollah's weapons and also demanded Israel withdraw from the country's south.
In a speech on the eve of Lebanon's 83rd independence anniversary, Aoun vowed to press ahead with plans to bring all weapons under state control.
Lebanon's sovereignty still faces two threats, he said: "The Israeli occupation of parts of our territory" and foreign interference from "influential elements within the Iranian regime" through weapons and decisions outside the authority of the Lebanese state.
On Israel, Aoun stressed Lebanon's message was clear and direct: "Withdraw from every inch of Lebanese territory. Stop your attacks."
There would be "no occupation ever again", he said. "And no weapons outside the state that... serve the interests of, foreign powers," he added, without naming a specific group.
Such weapons may once have served a purpose, he said, but later imposed a high cost on Lebanon when they came to serve causes beyond its borders.
"You must hand over your weapons," Aoun said.
The Lebanese government has committed to disarming Hezbollah, whose arsenal has long outstripped that of the national army and which has justified its weapons as necessary to resist Israel.
In June, Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement that included the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual Israeli withdrawal from territories it occupies in the south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the area.
But implementation has stalled and Hezbollah has refused to surrender its weapons.
Israel's army still carries out strikes, shelling and detonations in the south, where its forces are operating in a self-declared "security zone" running around 10 kilometres.
Report by AFP

Pezeshkian says Iran engaged in 'silent economic war' as blockade completes 130 days
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said that his country was engaged in a "silent war that is far more difficult than the one in which missiles are launched and destruction is inflicted".
In a video shared by Al Jazeera, Pezeshkian said: "It is an economic war, one that you, as those working on the economic front, are dealing with. It is by no means an easy one."
While the Iranian economy has been under duress for years in the face of international sanctions, this year’s US naval blockade on Iranian oil and new sanctions imposed since the start of the war have increased the pressure manifold.
Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs, on Saturday described the naval blockade an act of war, vowing that the country would take action to break it, according to Mehr news agency.
On Saturday, the US Central Command said "today marks 130 consecutive days of America's blockade against Iran".
"US service members are enforcing the blockade with exceptional focus, determination, and professionalism — preventing Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps from exporting billions of dollars in crude oil," Centcom said on X.
